segments.text: We often talk about AI as if it's a sentient being, but it's actually more like a giant calculator
running math at a scale we can't visualize. And that calculator just solved a problem
that had beaten biology for 50 years. To see how, we have to look at proteins.
Think of them as the microscopic machines that run your body,
digesting food, carrying oxygen, and fighting off infections. Each protein starts as a long
it folds into a specific three-dimensional shape. In biology, shape is everything. Diseases
are often the result of protein shapes gone wrong, and drugs are just shapes designed to block them.
Because shape dictates function, predicting how these strings fold gives us a direct blueprint
for understanding how to fight disease. But the math is nearly impossible. A medium-sized protein
can fold in more ways than there are atoms in the universe. Global lab work tried to brute force
the answer for half a century. In 50 years, humans managed to solve about 200,000 protein shapes.
That left hundreds of millions of shapes unsolved. For decades, this lack of data
created a massive bottleneck in medical research. Biology had hit a mathematical wall. There were
simply too many possibilities for humans to search by hand. The solution didn't start in a lab.
It started with a teenager who loved games.
Demis Hasabes was a chess master at 13, and by 17, he was co-designing video games that sold
millions of copies. He spent the next two decades pivoting to science, earning a PhD in neuroscience
to understand the brain, then founding an AI company called DeepMind, which Google acquired in 2014.
In 2020, DeepMind pointed their AI at the protein folding problem. They essentially finished
the mystery, producing predictions as accurate as real lab experiments. Solving the 50-year
mystery didn't require a chemistry lab. It required an outsider's obsession with building a better
calculating machine. Then came the part that actually mattered. DeepMind didn't patent the
discovery. They gave the answers away for free. This scoreboard shows the difference in scale.
50 years of human lab work produced 200,000 shapes. DeepMind's single release in 2022
provided 200 million. That's a 1,000 times multiplier in a single go, released for free to the entire
world. In 2024, that impact earned Hasabes the Nobel Prize in chemistry. The computation was a
triumph, but the real impact came from the decision to release the results, instantly accelerating
research for millions of people. We are now seeing this pattern repeat. People are pointing
this pattern matching machine at problems with too many variables for humans to solve alone.
These are results you can see today. In medicine, AI screened thousands of compounds to find a
new antibiotic for a resistant superbug. And DeepMind has predicted 380,000 new crystals
to help build better batteries and solar panels. In a Swedish trial, AI caught 20% more
breast cancers than radiologists working alone. It's also accelerating physical science,
global weather forecasts that used to take hours now take one minute. There are also tools
shipping right now for accessibility, like free software that reads the world for blind users,
or provides live captions for the deaf. When people ask what good AI actually does for society,
you have an answer. It's important to remember that this didn't start with a piece of software.
It started with a kid who loved chess and a deliberate choice of where the focus.
Rare brilliance is one thing, but the attitude to point that talent toward helping people
is a choice anyone can make. Whatever you are good at, point it at something that helps people.
The big upside is happening today. AI is already accelerating work that protects and improves lives.
